title: Modern states, nations and empires
summary: The modern state did not mark the first appearance of powerful government. It changed the distance between government and society. Registration, education, administration and common rules brought states into more direct relationships with their populations.

blocks.text: The modern state did not mark the first appearance of powerful government. It changed the distance between government and society. Registration, education, administration and common rules brought states into more direct relationships with their populations.

Nationalism organized language, history and political belonging into mass identities. Schools, records and public narratives helped strangers imagine a shared community while defining who belonged and who was excluded. Common identity was not without boundaries.

Bureaucracy sustained activity through offices, archives and expertise, while industrial technology expanded transport, military and resource-mobilizing capabilities. These could support domestic construction or control over distant places.

Nation-states and empires therefore did not simply replace one another in sequence. The industrial era could expand civic politics alongside overseas domination. Understanding modern capabilities requires asking who controlled them and how they were used, rather than deriving outcomes from institutional names.
